slides.title: Chapter 14: Second-Layer Apps
slides.sub: What the chain guarantees, how a payment channel is built, and how Lightning routes payments

items.body: Picture: the Bitcoin logo, public domain (Wikimedia Commons). Python 3.14.6; Bitcoin Core 31.1 and lnd 0.21.3-beta results are one recorded run, read back here.

slides.notes: This opening slide names the chapter and its question: what can be built on top of Bitcoin without changing its rules. The chapter covers the guarantees of the chain, colored coins, payment channels and the Lightning Network, which together make up the second layer. Every number you will meet on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library or read from one recorded run of Bitcoin Core and lnd on private test chains. Mastering Bitcoin, third edition, chapter 14 is the source text, and the course page reruns every example.

slides.sub: Four parts; every number is a slide you can jump to

slides.notes: The route has four parts, and they follow the order of the chapter: what the chain guarantees, colored coins and seals, payment channels, and the Lightning Network. Nineteen code examples and four true stories are spread across the parts. The examples are listed in the same order in the Run slide code menu of the course page, so each listing can be run and edited there. Use this slide to see where a topic sits in the whole route before you open its part.
slides.take: Four parts, nineteen examples, four true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

items: Which guarantees of the chain can an application rely on, and how do two applications mix them?
How can a coin carry a second meaning, and who checks it?
What does a payment channel put on the chain, and what stays off it?
How does a revocation key stop a party from cheating with an old state?
How does an HTLC let a secret open a payment and time return it?
How does Lightning route a payment through strangers and keep the route private?
What does a channel cost, and what does a relay earn?

slides.notes: These seven questions are the chapter's own questions, rewritten so that each has an answer on a named slide. They run from the guarantees of the chain to the cost of a channel and the earnings of a relay. Read them first and try to answer each one from what you already know, then return to them in the summary slide at the end. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter. The course page offers a quiz on the same questions.

slides.title: What the chain guarantees
slides.sub: Applications reuse the chain's guarantees: no double spend, a trusted date, and a signature that only the key holder can make.

items.meaning: Guarantees such as no double spend and immutability can be reused by any application.
A digital notary and a crowdfund each mix several guarantees.

slides.notes: Bitcoin offers guarantees that any application can reuse: no double spend, immutability, a trusted timestamp and more. Software built on them is called a second-layer application, because it changes none of the chain's rules. The two columns name the two ideas of this part: the building blocks themselves, and applications such as a digital notary or a crowdfund that combine several of them. Four of the guarantees are tested on a private chain in the code slides that follow. For the full list see chapter 14 of Mastering Bitcoin.

slides.title: A double spend and the fee
slides.sub: Two spends of one coin on a private chain

rows: fees = [d['fee_%s_sat' % k] for k in ks]
groups.note: Bitcoin Core, on a private chain, accepted a first spend of one coin.
A second spend of the same coin with a lower fee was refused, with a named reason.
A second spend with a higher fee replaced the first, and the first vanished.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: fee of each spend, in satoshis
The lower fee is refused: insufficient fee. The higher fee wins, and the first spend is gone: yes.

slides.notes: No output can be spent twice in the same valid chain, and this slide shows how the network enforces it. Bitcoin Core, running on a private chain, accepted a first spend of one coin and refused a second spend that paid a lower fee, with a named reason in its reply. A second spend that paid a higher fee replaced the first one, and the first then vanished from the waiting pool. The bar chart shows the three fees in satoshis. This is example 1 in the Run slide code menu; related ideas are replace-by-fee in chapter 9.
slides.take: Only a spend that pays more can replace the first one

slides.title: Two pizzas for 10,000 bitcoins
slides.sub: The first purchase settled on the chain; small ones now travel off it

items.cap: Papa Johns Jacksonville - Sanjev Rajaram, CC0 1.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: On 22 May 2010 Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas, the first notable retail purchase of physical goods with bitcoin.
He had offered the coins for a couple of pizzas in a Bitcoin Forum post, and a 19-year-old, Jeremy Sturdivant, took the offer.
Sturdivant ordered two Papa John's pizzas to Hanyecz's home in Jacksonville and received the coins; the payment settled on the chain.
A payment on the chain waits for confirmations, which payment channels and Lightning avoid for small payments.

items.body: Picture: the plaque in a Papa John's shop

items.who: Laszlo Hanyecz, a programmer who posted the offer and had contributed to Bitcoin's source code, and Jeremy Sturdivant
items.where: Jacksonville, Florida, USA, where the pizzas were delivered, and the Bitcoin Forum, where the offer was posted

slides.notes: This true story dates the first purchase of a physical good with bitcoin. On 22 May 2010 the programmer Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas, after offering the coins in a forum post; a 19-year-old named Jeremy Sturdivant took the offer and ordered the pizzas from Papa John's in Jacksonville, Florida. The payment settled on the chain and waited for confirmations. That wait is why small everyday payments now travel through channels and the Lightning Network, which later slides explain. The link on the slide leads to the original forum thread.

slides.title: What the chain guarantees: concepts (2 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: a concept of the chapter and its meaning

items.label: authorization
items.meaning: A script that asks for a signature cannot run without the holder of the private key.

items.label: consistency
items.meaning: The deeper a block lies, the less likely it is to be reorganised.

items.label: forgery protection
items.meaning: A transaction can spend only existing, validated outputs, so value cannot be counterfeited.

items.label: immutability
items.meaning: The more work lies on top of a transaction, the more energy it takes to rewrite it.

items.label: integrity
items.meaning: A signature covers the parts of a transaction it commits to, so they cannot be altered.

items.label: neutrality
items.meaning: The network relays any valid transaction with a sufficient fee, whoever sends it.

slides.title: Nonexpiration and accounting guarantees
slides.sub: A transaction signed long ago, and one that pays too much

groups.note: A transaction signed 150 blocks earlier was still accepted, because its input was unspent.
A transaction whose outputs exceed its inputs is refused, whatever its signatures say.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: two guarantees put to the test
The old transaction is still valid. The one that pays out more than it takes in is refused with the name bad-txns-in-belowout.

slides.notes: Two further guarantees are tested here. Nonexpiration means that a valid transaction stays valid for as long as its input is unspent: a transaction signed 150 blocks earlier was still accepted by the test node. Accounting means that outputs never exceed inputs, so a transaction cannot create value: one that paid out more than it took in was refused, whatever its signatures said, with the reason bad-txns-in-belowout. The table shows both results. Connect this slide with the concept cards on accounting and nonexpiration, and with example 2 of the Run slide code menu.
slides.take: A transaction does not expire, and it can never pay out more than it takes in

slides.title: Proof of existence with a hash
slides.sub: A document's hash in an OP_RETURN output

groups.note: A transaction can carry the hash of a document in an output that nobody can spend.
The script is OP_RETURN followed by the hash, and the output holds no value.
The block that holds the transaction gives the document a date.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the notary output
The hash is in the chain at block 452, dated 2026-10-15. The document itself is not in the chain.

slides.notes: Proof of existence is the guarantee that a hash in a transaction proves a document existed when the block holding it was mined. The code builds an output whose script is OP_RETURN followed by the hash of a document; such an output holds no value and nobody can spend it. The block gives the hash its date, here block 452, while the document itself never enters the chain. This is how a digital notary can be built from the guarantees of timestamping and immutability. It is example 3 in the Run slide code menu.
slides.take: A hash in a transaction proves that the document existed at that block's date

slides.title: What the chain guarantees: concepts (4 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: a concept of the chapter and its meaning

items.label: recording external state
items.meaning: A transaction can commit to outside data through OP_RETURN or pay to contract.

items.label: replication
items.meaning: Every full node keeps a copy of the chain, so the data survives local failures.

items.label: second layer
items.meaning: A system that settles on the chain but does most of its work away from it.

items.label: secure timestamping
items.meaning: The consensus rules keep block times roughly honest, so a recorded fact has a trusted date.

items.label: timelock
items.meaning: A script clause can run only after a set time or block height.

items.label: transaction atomicity
items.meaning: A transaction is mined in full or not at all, never halfway.

slides.title: Lighthouse: a crowdfund on the chain
slides.sub: Pledges that move only when the goal is met

groups.note: Two pledges, less the fee, make the goal of the fundraiser.
One pledge alone is refused; both pledges together are accepted.
Changing the output breaks the signatures, and a signature of everything stops a late pledge.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: four tries at the fundraiser
The fundraiser can be spent only with all pledges in and the output unchanged.

slides.notes: Lighthouse is a crowdfunding application whose pledges are signed inputs that become spendable only when the goal is met. In the code, two pledges less the fee make the goal. One pledge alone is refused, because it pays out more than it takes in, and both together are accepted. Changing the output breaks the signatures, and a signature over every input and output stops a pledge that comes too late. The table lists four tries. This shows how the guarantees of authorization and integrity combine; see example 4 of the Run slide code menu.
slides.take: Signatures fix the output, so the money moves only when the goal is reached

slides.title: Colored coins and seals
slides.sub: A colored coin ties a statement about another asset to an output; the chain commits, the receiver checks the rest.

items.meaning: An unspent output can be tied to a statement only once, when it is spent.
A key is tweaked so that it commits to a contract nobody else sees.
The receiver checks the whole history of an asset; the chain holds only commitments.

slides.notes: Colored coins are the second part of the chapter: a small amount of bitcoin is marked so that it stands for another asset, such as a share. Three ideas make that possible. A single-use seal is tied to an unspent output and opens only once, a public key can be tweaked so that it commits to a contract, and the receiver checks the whole history of the asset because the chain holds only commitments. Two of the three ideas are run in the code slides of this part. Chapter 14 of the book describes RGB and Taproot Assets.

slides.title: Client-side validation of a token history
slides.sub: A token history that the chain never shows

rows: outs = len({h['outpoint'] for h in c['history']})
groups.note: The history of ACME tokens names two transactions and three outputs.
Each step commits to its contract; a forged contract does not match.
Yet nothing in the chain shows that any token exists.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the history of the ACME tokens
The chain shows ordinary outputs only. The receiver must read the history to know what they mean.

slides.notes: Client-side validation means the receiver checks the whole history of an asset, because the chain stores only commitments. The code builds the history of ACME tokens, which passes through two transactions and three outputs. Each step commits to its contract, and a forged contract does not match its commitment. Yet nothing in the chain shows that any token exists, so the receiver must read the history to know what the outputs mean. The table shows what the chain sees and what the receiver must verify. slides.title: Pay to contract: a tweaked key
slides.sub: A tweaked key that commits to a contract

groups.note: A key tweaked by a contract gives another address than the plain key.
Revealing the contract and the tweak proves the commitment; a wrong contract fails.
Only the tweaked key can spend the output; the plain key cannot.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: a key tweaked by a contract
The reveal proves the commitment only for the real contract, and only the tweaked key spends.

slides.notes: Pay to contract tweaks a public key with a contract, so the key commits to an agreement that nobody else sees and looks like any other key. The code shows that a tweaked key gives a different address from the plain key. Revealing the contract and the tweak proves the commitment, a wrong contract fails the proof, and only the tweaked key can spend the output; the plain key cannot. Connect this with single-use seals and with taproot, where a similar tweak commits to a script tree. It is example 6 of the Run slide code menu.
slides.take: Only the holder of the contract can reveal the commitment and spend

slides.title: Payment channels: trade often, settle once
slides.sub: A channel puts two transactions on the chain, the funding and the settlement, and keeps every update in between off it.

items.meaning: Two transactions on the chain, and any number of signed updates between them.
Each side's payout is delayed, and an old state can be punished with a revocation key.
A secret claims the payment before a deadline; after it the payer takes the money back.

slides.notes: Payment channels are the third part. Two people can trade many times and settle once, because only the funding and the settlement need to touch the chain. This part builds a channel step by step: a funding output that needs both keys, refunds with falling lock times, balances that move while capacity stays fixed, commitments that punish an old state, and a hash time lock that lets a secret claim a payment. Each step is run on a private chain with Bitcoin Core, and the chapter text gives the formal description.

items.label: Making Trustless Channels

slides.title: Emma and Fabian's channel
slides.sub: A two-of-two output funded by Emma

groups.note: Emma funds one hour of video at 1,000 satoshis a second: 3,600,000 satoshis.
Spending the funding output needs both signatures; Emma alone is refused.
The script starts with 2 and ends with 2 and CHECKMULTISIG: two of two.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the funding output of the channel
Opcode 52 is OP_2 and ae is CHECKMULTISIG: two keys must sign, so Emma cannot run off with the funds.

slides.notes: A payment channel starts with a funding output. In the example Emma funds one hour of video at 1,000 satoshis a second, which is 3,600,000 satoshis. The funding output is a two-of-two multisignature script, so spending it needs both signatures and Emma alone is refused. The witness script begins with the number 2 and ends with 2 and CHECKMULTISIG; in the table opcode 52 is OP_2 and ae is CHECKMULTISIG. This is the quorum-of-control guarantee at work, and example 7 of the Run slide code menu runs it.
slides.take: The funding output needs both keys, so neither side can spend alone

slides.title: The first payment channels
slides.sub: Channels began as a replaced transaction waiting for its lock time

items.cap: Micropayment channel - Burchert, Decker, Wattenhofer, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: Mike Hearn posted Anti DoS for tx replacement on 17 April 2013, and Jeremy Spillman answered on 20 April with a one-way channel design.
The first Bitcoin code already let an unrecorded open transaction be replaced until its lock time, and the channel idea grew from that.
The payer signs larger and larger payments while a refund waits behind a lock time; Hearn and Matt Corallo announced bitcoinj code on 27 June 2013.
Such channels were safe only with segwit transactions, so Emma's refund is signed before the funding is sent.

items.body: Picture: a later authors' channel diagram

items.who: Mike Hearn, who posted Anti DoS for tx replacement on 17 April 2013, Jeremy Spillman, who answered on 20 April 2013, and Matt Corallo
items.where: the bitcoin-development mailing list, BitcoinTalk.org and the bitcoinj library
items.linkText: Reply: Anti DoS for tx replacement (list post)

slides.notes: This true story traces where payment channels came from. The Bitcoin Wiki and the first Bitcoin code describe an unrecorded transaction that could be replaced until its lock time. In April 2013 Mike Hearn posted about replacing transactions and Jeremy Spillman answered with a one-way channel design, in which the payer signs larger and larger payments while a refund waits behind a lock time. Hearn and Matt Corallo announced bitcoinj code in June 2013. Such channels were safe only with segwit transactions, which is why Emma signs her refund before sending the funding. The slide links to the sources.

slides.title: Payment channels: key concepts (2 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: a concept of the chapter and its meaning

items.label: State Channels - Basic Concepts and Terminology
items.meaning: A funding transaction opens the channel, commitments change it, and a settlement closes it.

items.label: asymmetric commitment
items.meaning: The two commitments differ: the holder's own payout waits, the other side is paid at once.

items.label: commitment transaction
items.meaning: A signed transaction that could be published but is held back and replaced by newer ones.

items.label: funding transaction
items.meaning: The one transaction that locks the shared funds in a two-of-two output and opens the channel.

items.label: payment channel
items.meaning: Two parties keep a running balance of signed transactions that they do not publish.

items.label: preimage
items.meaning: The secret that hashes to the value in an HTLC; whoever knows it can claim the payment.

slides.title: Refunds with falling lock times
slides.sub: Six signed refunds; the newest becomes valid first

groups.note: Six refunds were signed, each with a lower lock time than the one before.
At the start every one of them is refused as not yet final.
The newest refund is refused six blocks early and accepted five blocks before.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: six refunds signed before funding
Six blocks early the newest refund is not yet final; five blocks early it is accepted.

slides.notes: A channel needs a way out if the other party disappears, and this slide builds it. Emma signs six refunds before she funds the channel, each with a lower lock time than the one before, so the newest refund becomes valid first. At the start every refund is refused as not yet final. Six blocks before the newest lock time it is still refused, and five blocks before it is accepted. The table shows the six lock times. The idea combines the timelock guarantee with the earlier funding output. It is example 8 of the Run slide code menu.
slides.take: The newest refund has the lowest lock time, so it can be used first

slides.title: Payment channels: key concepts (3 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: a concept of the chapter and its meaning

items.label: refund transaction
items.meaning: A signed, time-locked transaction that returns the funds if the channel never starts.

items.label: revocation key
items.meaning: A key of two secret halves that lets the wronged side take the whole channel after a cheat.

items.label: settlement transaction
items.meaning: The final transaction that closes the channel and pays each side its share.

slides.title: Balances move, capacity stays
slides.sub: A channel of 100 units after three payments

groups.note: A channel of 100 units starts with everything on Alice's side.

rows: tot = {a + b for a, b in hist}
left = [a for a, b in hist]
groups.note: Each move shifts value between the two sides; their sum never changes.
The left column is Alice's balance after each step, and the sum stays at 100.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: Alice's balance after each payment
Bob holds the rest each time. The two balances always add up to 100.

slides.notes: The capacity of a channel is fixed when it is funded, and payments only move value between the two sides. In the example a channel of 100 units starts with everything on Alice's side. Each move shifts value to Bob, and the sum of the two balances stays at 100 after every step; the chart shows Alice's balance falling. A payment larger than the sender's balance cannot be made. This explains why a channel's capacity limits the largest payment it can carry, which matters again for routing in the Lightning part. It is example 9 of the Run slide code menu.

slides.title: On the chain, or off it?
slides.sub: Why a channel is cheap and fast, and what it still needs from the chain

left.head: On the chain
rows: The funding transaction opens the channel.
The settlement closes it for good.

right.head: Off the chain
rows: No one else sees them, and fees are small.

slides.notes: A channel puts exactly two transactions on the chain: the funding transaction that opens it and the settlement that closes it for good. Everything between them stays off the chain as signed commitments that change the balances. No one else sees these updates and their fees are small. The chain acts as the court of last resort, which is why each side keeps its latest commitment and must be able to publish it. Compare the two columns and remember the rule: two transactions on the chain, any number of updates between them.
slides.take: Two transactions on the chain, and any number of updates between them

slides.title: A commitment that can be punished
slides.sub: The delayed output of a commitment transaction

groups.note: The delayed output is an IF branch: revocation key, or a wait.
The delayed spend fails at 999 confirmations, passes at 1,000.
Revocation needs both halves of the key; one half fails.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the delayed output of a commitment
The cheater must wait 1000 blocks, while the victim holding both halves can take the output at once.

slides.notes: A commitment transaction must be punishable, otherwise a party could publish an old state. The delayed output has two spending paths: a revocation key that works at once, or a wait of 1,000 blocks. At 999 confirmations the delayed spend is refused and at 1,000 it is accepted. The revocation path needs both halves of the key, so one half alone fails. A cheater must therefore wait a thousand blocks, while the victim, who holds both halves after the revocation, can take the output immediately. It is example 10 of the Run slide code menu.
slides.take: A cheater waits a thousand blocks, and the victim can act before that

slides.title: An HTLC: a secret or the clock
slides.sub: Who can claim a hash time lock contract, and when

groups.note: The right secret and the receiver's key claim the output; the payer's key does not.
The refund works only at the lock height, nineteen blocks after funding.
A wrong secret fails the hash check, whoever signs.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: who can claim the HTLC
The secret opens it for the receiver. The clock opens it for the payer, but only at the lock height.

slides.notes: A hash time lock contract, or HTLC, lets a secret claim a payment before a deadline, and lets the payer take the money back afterwards. In the example the receiver claims the output with the right secret and a signature. A wrong secret fails the hash check whoever signs, and the payer's key cannot claim it. The payer's refund becomes final only at the lock height, nineteen blocks after funding. HTLCs are the building block that Lightning uses to route a payment across many channels, which the next part shows. It is example 11 of the Run slide code menu.
slides.take: A secret claims the payment; after the lock height the payer takes it back

slides.title: The Lightning Network: payments across channels
slides.sub: Lightning routes a payment across many channels, and each relay keeps a small fee for forwarding it.

items.meaning: A payment crosses several channels, and each relay keeps a small fee.
The sender wraps the path in layers, and each relay peels exactly one.
A payee's invoice names an amount and a hash; the BOLTs are the shared standards.

slides.notes: The Lightning Network is the fourth part. It links payment channels end to end so that anyone can pay anyone through intermediaries, and every relay keeps a small fee for forwarding. The three columns name the three ideas of the part: routing and fees, onion routing in which the sender wraps the path in layers and each relay peels exactly one, and invoices together with the BOLT standards that let different programs work together. Every number in the code slides comes from the recorded run of five lnd nodes or from the specifications.

slides.title: Satoshis passed from hand to hand
slides.sub: Satoshis passed hand to hand without touching the chain

items.cap: Jack Dorsey 2009 - Brian Solis, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: On 19 January 2019 the Twitter user hodlonaut began a game-like test of Lightning by sending 100,000 satoshis to a trusted recipient.
It was a promotional test, passed from one well-known person to the next, to show that the network could carry real payments.
Each recipient added 10,000 satoshis, 34 cents then, and sent the sum on; Jack Dorsey, Charlie Lee, Elizabeth Stark and Changpeng Zhao took part.
Each hand-over was an ordinary Lightning payment, with no transaction on the chain for each step.

items.body: Picture: Jack Dorsey, 2009, a recipient

items.who: hodlonaut, a pseudonymous Twitter user who began the game, and the recipients who passed it on, among them Jack Dorsey, Charlie Lee
items.where: Twitter, and the Lightning Network, where each payment was sent

slides.notes: This true story shows Lightning carrying real value for the first time as a game. On 19 January 2019 the pseudonymous Twitter user hodlonaut began a promotional test by sending 100,000 satoshis to a trusted recipient. Each recipient added 10,000 satoshis, worth 34 cents then, and sent the sum on; Jack Dorsey, Charlie Lee, Elizabeth Stark and Changpeng Zhao took part. Each hand-over was an ordinary Lightning payment, with no transaction on the chain for each step, which is the point of the second layer. The slide links to the original thread.

slides.title: Each hop has less time
slides.sub: The expiry of the HTLC on each hop

groups.note: The HTLC of each hop expires at a block height, and the earliest expiry is at Eric's end.

rows: gap = [p - q for p, q in zip(e, e[1:])]
groups.note: The gap between neighbours is 80 blocks, so a relay can always reclaim in time.
The library rebuilds the expiries from the last hop backwards.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: blocks left until the HTLC of each hop expires
Neighbours differ by 80 blocks, and the last two share one expiry. The library agrees: yes.

slides.notes: A relay must always be able to reclaim its money upstream after it pays downstream, and time locks guarantee that. Every hop's HTLC expires at a block height, and the earliest expiry is at Eric's end. Neighbouring hops differ by 80 blocks, so a relay that pays downstream and then learns the secret still has time to claim from upstream; the last two hops share one expiry. The library rebuilds the same heights from the last hop backwards. The chart shows the blocks left on each hop. It is example 13 of the Run slide code menu.

slides.title: A paper that became a network
slides.sub: A design on paper took years, soft forks and four teams

items.cap: Lightning cut nodes - FrankAndProust, CC0 1.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja published a Lightning Network white paper in February 2015; the draft kept on lightning.network is version 0.5.9.2.
Their summary calls it a decentralized system for instant, high-volume micropayments that removes the risk of trusting third-party custody.
Lightning Labs launched the network in 2018; the picture shows its cut nodes, from under 100 in 2018 to about 1,500 in 2022.
The book says the network was first described in February 2015; the word proposed no longer holds.

items.body: Picture: the network's cut nodes, approximate

items.who: Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja, the authors of the Lightning Network paper, and Lightning Labs, which launched the network in 2018

slides.notes: This true story records how a design on paper became a network. Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja published the Lightning Network white paper in February 2015, describing a decentralized system for instant, high-volume micropayments that removes the risk of trusting third-party custody. It took years, soft forks and four independent teams before Lightning Labs launched the network in 2018. The picture shows its cut nodes growing from under 100 in 2018 to about 1,500 in 2022, read approximately from the chart. The book says the network was first described in 2015; the word proposed no longer holds.

slides.notes: A hold invoice keeps a payment waiting in flight. Eric held back the secret, so the payment stayed pending along all four channels: one HTLC at each end and two at each relay, as the chart counts. When Eric cancelled, every balance returned to where it began. A later payment of the same kind settled once the secret was released. This shows that a Lightning payment is either claimed in full or returned, the property called atomicity, and that a pending payment holds balances in the channels it crosses. slides.title: The onion has a fixed size
slides.sub: The parts of a BOLT 4 packet

groups.note: A packet holds a version byte, a key, the hop data and a check value.
The specification says one packet of 1366 bytes, whatever the route.
Its limit is twenty hops, so a relay cannot tell how far the end is.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the BOLT 4 packet
Hop data takes 1,300 of 1,366 bytes. It is padded, so a short route looks like a long one.

slides.notes: Lightning uses onion routing so that no relay learns the whole path. A BOLT 4 packet holds a version byte, a key, 1,300 bytes of hop data and a check value, which makes 1,366 bytes whatever the route. The limit is twenty hops, and the hop data is padded, so a short route looks like a long one and a relay cannot tell how far it is from the end. The table lists the parts and their sizes. Connect this slide with the privacy benefit named on the concept cards. It is example 16 of the Run slide code menu.
slides.take: The packet is 1366 bytes whatever the route, so a relay cannot count the hops

slides.title: A breach and its punishment
slides.sub: The justice transaction, and a fee paid by a child

groups.note: Irene went back to an old state and published it; Hitesh's node saw the breach.
The last state owed Hitesh 700,000,000 satoshis, yet the justice transaction paid him the whole channel.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the breach and the fee bump

slides.notes: A channel must punish cheating, and this example shows it end to end. Irene went back to an old state and published it. Hitesh's node saw the breach, and its justice transaction took the whole channel, although the last state owed Hitesh only 700,000,000 satoshis. A second test showed that a parent transaction with no fee can be lifted into a block by a child that pays for both, a technique called child pays for parent. Connect this with the revocation key of slide 29 and with watchtowers in the further reading. It is example 19.
slides.take: A cheater loses the whole channel, and a child can pay the parent's fee

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per idea, each provable from its slides

items: The chain guarantees no double spend, immutability and more, and applications are recipes that mix these guarantees.
Colored coins use a single-use seal, a contract-committing key and client-side checks, so the chain never sees the asset.
A payment channel needs two transactions on the chain, and signed commitments in between.
A revocation key punishes an old state, and an HTLC lets a secret claim a payment before a deadline.
Lightning routes a payment through relays that each keep a fee and have less time than the one before.

slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature, one for each part of the chapter and one for the idea that joins them. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed there. The first line gathers the guarantees of the chain, the second colored coins, the third the two transactions of a channel, the fourth the revocation key and the HTLC, and the fifth routing with fees and falling time limits. The Run slide code menu reruns all nineteen examples.
slides.take: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt
